rows.summary: The compiler catches the habits of TypeScript, Dart and Python (`N0022`, with an exact `fix`), invented classes (`N0220`) and invented named arguments (`N0219`, it lists the real ones).
body: The compiler catches the habits of TypeScript, Dart and Python (`N0022`, with an exact `fix`), invented classes
(`N0220`) and invented named arguments (`N0219`, it lists the real ones). Apply the fix instead of rewriting.
- Writing `return`, `;`, `{ }`, `new`, `await`, `const`/`final`/`var`, `&&`, `!x`, `name: value` arguments: use the
sheet's forms (`~x`, `x = 1`, `and`, `not x`, `name = value`).
- The return type goes after the parameters: `load(id: int) User`.
- In Dragonfly, a screen calls its `statemanager`, which calls the component's `appcomponent`; only the use case
calls the repository. Another component sees only the `appcomponent`, models, events, guards and screens.
- Texts shown to the user are translation keys: `"component.screen.key".tr()` plus the key in
`assets/i18n/<locale>/<component>.json`.

round. The user chose **retrieval plus distillation** instead: a frontier model answers a task bank once, its answers
that pass the compiler become examples in the knowledge base, and the local model is measured against it until its
answers are equivalent.

body: 1. **Nuclear Smart Graph** (`nuclear-graph`, its own repository): the knowledge base of the whole ecosystem in Chroma,
with vectors from a local embeddings model (EmbeddingGemma on Ollama). Four collections: `knowledge` (every spec,
guide, context file, ADR, dialect word, example and the CLIs' help, made by `ingest` and refreshed by hash),
`examples` (validated task → solution pairs), `prompts` (the validated prompt of each use case), `memory` (what an
agent keeps about a project).
2. **The graph is private.** Only its server process opens the store. It listens on 127.0.0.1 and answers only with a
token; each program asks for access and the user allows it (`nuclear-graph allow`, `connect`); tokens are kept as
hashes, with scopes `read`, `write`, `admin`; requests with an `Origin` header (a web page) are refused; documents
are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, the key and the owner's token live in the desktop keyring (`secret-tool`),
the data folder is 0700; only `ingest` (the owner) writes `knowledge`.
3. **One MCP server for NuclearLang** (`nuclear-graph mcp`, stdio): the graph (`graph_search`, `graph_prompt`,
`graph_remember`), the compiler (`nuclear_check`, `nuclear_build`, `nuclear_help`, `nuclear_brief`, `nuclear_fmt`,
`nuclear_defs`), the `dragonfly` commands of a project (an allow list) and the local developer

4. **Nuclear Developer** (`nuclear-developer`, its own repository) is a Dragonfly backend written in Nuclear (fastapi
dialect): four LangGraph graphs (coder, tester, security reviewer, planner) on `qwen2.5-coder:3b` and `gemma4:e2b`.
A small model follows steps better than it chooses tools, so each graph runs fixed steps: recall from the graph
(the use case's prompt, knowledge, solved examples, example files) → write → `nuclear check` → repair with the
compiler's errors (at most three attempts). Each HTTP request runs on its own thread. Its tools reach the graph and
the compiler through `nuclear_graph.client` and `nuclear_graph.toolchain`, whose type definitions the project keeps
in `defs/`.
5. **The evaluation is the training loop** (`nuclear-developer/eval`): a bank of tasks with acceptance texts, split
into `train` (their frontier answers become graph examples) and `test` (held out); an answer passes when `nuclear
check` reports no errors and it has every acceptance text; the local developer is equivalent to the frontier model
on a task when both pass. A failure is fixed by adding a general rule or knowledge to the graph, never the answer.

rows.title: ADR-0104: The Smart Graph is a library of typed, linked, versioned rows — Decision
rows.summary: 7. Versions.
body: 7. **Versions.** `manifest.json` holds the schema (the row format; it changes when an old row could not be read), the
revision (one more whenever any row changes, is added or is removed), each row's hash and the revision that last
changed it, and for each curated row the hash of each of its `sources` (a file, or `file#Heading` for one section)
at its last review. `revisions.json` is the log. An ingest writes the schema and the revision into the collections'
metadata; `GET /v1/stats` and `nuclear-graph stats` say which revision the graph holds.
8. **The base never stays behind the code.** `nuclear-graph knowledge check` fails when a generated file is not what
the tree gives now, when a row is invalid, when the manifest is of other rows, when a source of a curated row
changed since its review, or when the running graph holds another revision. The end-of-turn hook of the working
tree (`tools/context/check.sh stop`) runs it: a session that changed the ecosystem cannot finish while it fails.
The procedure is itself a row (`playbook:update-the-knowledge-base`): build, review the rows whose sources changed
(update them, or `knowledge review <id>` when they still hold), check, ingest. A row written by hand is reviewed
when it is written or changed.

rows.summary: 2. A row is a card.
body: 2. **A row is a card.** `id` (`<prefix>:<name>`: `error:N0114`, `kind:backend.usecase`, `tool:dragonfly.gen.resource`,
`concept:mcp`; a prefix belongs to one shelf, so an id is fetched without a search), `type`, `title`, `summary`
(the answer in a sentence or two), `body` (the whole card), `keys` (exact names in lower case), `asks` (questions
it answers, as people write them), `tags`, `platforms`, `agents`, `links` (`{rel, to}`), `sources`, `meta` (the
shelf's own filters), `data`.
- In Chroma, the metadata (in clear, as the vectors are): `card`, `facet`, `type`, `title`, `agents`, `platforms`
(`["all"]` when the row is of every platform), `keys`, `tags`, `links` (the ids it points to, so "who links to
X" is a filter), `origin`, `source`, `hash`, `rev`, and the shelf's own. The document (encrypted): the card.
- What is embedded is not the document: the title goes in the embedding model's title slot, with the summary and
the first 1200 characters of the body as its text. Each `ask` is one more entry of the collection (`facet: ask`)
that points to its card: a question finds the card whose author wrote that question.

rows.title: ADR-0104: The Smart Graph is a library of typed, linked, versioned rows — Decision

body: 3. **Search is by meaning and by exact name, over several shelves** (`retrieve.py`). The query is embedded once and

whatever its language. Entries are ranked together, each card once; a `docs` row yields to a card (0.04) and a
document gives at most two sections. `expand` adds to each card the title and summary of the rows it links to.

Chroma keeps of every item a filter matches is compared with the query's (`Store.near`, `Store.measure`); Chroma's

body: 1. **Shelves.** One Chroma collection per kind of question, each with its own row types and filters
(`nuclear_graph/shelves.py` is the schema; the base carries it as `schema.json`):
| Shelf | The question it answers | Row types |
| `concepts` | What is it, why does it exist, how does it work? | purpose, concept, theory, architecture, comparison, faq, term |
| `language` | How is it written in Nuclear? | guide, rule, library, reference |
| `platforms` | What does a platform have, and where does each thing go? | platform, kind, decorator, layout, plugin, spec |
| `tools` | What can run, and how is it called? | cli, mcp, http, generator, stage, agent, editor, service, component |

| `capabilities` | Can it be done, by NuclearLang or by this agent? | can, cannot, limit, agent-limit |
| `playbooks` | How is this task done, step by step, and by whom? | playbook, role, skill |
| `examples` | What does the code look like? | file, solved |
| `docs` | What does the full document say? | spec, adr, context, guide, readme, changelog, status, doc |

body: A whole system, one screen, a rename and a failing test are not done the same way. The graph holds a **strategy** for

| Family | Kinds of request |
| create | a whole system, a project, a component, a resource of another API, a stored resource, the app of a backend, only an interface, a repository, a use case, a route, one declaration |

| fix | it does not compile; a test fails; it does the wrong thing; it fails while running; the data does not match; a screen shows the wrong thing; the machine or a service fails |

straight to *Verification*. A rename plans and writes, and writes no test.
- **Where the pieces come from.** For a new feature the planner splits what the generators left. For a change of
something that exists (a field more, a column) the pieces are the files that declare it. For a rename a tool gives
every file that writes the name, already rewritten: no model writes.
- **What is asked first.** A stored resource without its fields, a rename without its two names, a bug without what
should happen: the analysis stops the run with the question. Nothing is guessed.
- **The wiring.** After *Code*, each use case the coder wrote is wired by `dragonfly gen usecase`: its alias in the
facade and, when the spec's sentence gives it (`POST orders/{id}/cancel`), its route.
- **A bug's repair** goes to the file the failure names, whoever wrote it, and never to the test.
A request that is not a run (a question, a command, something beyond the platform) stops at the analysis and says
where it belongs. The analysis read it wrong: name the strategy in the spec (`- Strategy: usecase`, under `- Use
case:`) and run it again.

rows.summary: with `--dry-run` first.
body: with `--dry-run` first. The fields come from
the spec's example answer or its `Key | Type` table, or from the API's own answer. The planner then plans only what
is left (often nothing), and a crash undoes the generated files like an agent's.
- **Plan** shows the work as a tree: the big parts (one per component), the tasks of each (a layer: data, domain, the
facade, the entry points, the tests) and the pieces of each task (one file). It also says, before any code, what
of the spec is beyond the platform or the local agents (the graph's capabilities whose trigger words the spec
writes: "authentication" on a backend, "form" on the web; a spec too long for a local model; a plan without pieces):
split the task, give the missing facts, or let a frontier model lead.
- **Tests first** is skipped when the generators wrote every file of the run: they wrote its tests too, and the step
says which. A resource that reads another API gets no generated test (it would call the real one): the step says
so, and only the acceptance step holds the criteria against the result.
- **Anything runs again.** *Run again from this step* on every step, passed or failed: it and every step after it
run again, the steps before it are kept. *Run <stage> again* on every stage. *Run again from scratch* on the run:

rows.title: AI loop: specs to deployed code, with local agents — 3. Follow the run
rows.summary: 1. Before anyone writes, the transpiler has written the project map (`.nuclear/map.md`): every declaration with its kind, its description (its `//` doc comment) and its members.
body: 1. Before anyone writes, the transpiler has written the **project map** (`.nuclear/map.md`): every declaration with
its kind, its description (its `//` doc comment) and its members. The agents read it instead of every file, so
give each declaration a one-line description.
2. **Tests first**: the tester writes one test per acceptance criterion with the names the plan gives.

3. **Code**: the coder writes each piece at its place (`nuclear help layout --platform

`), with the card of its
kind, the mistakes to avoid with that kind, examples of it and the project's files that declare the names its task
writes (it reads them by itself); the compiler checks it, then the whole project.
4. **Verification**: every test runs. A failing test goes back to the coder told in Nuclear (`dragonfly explain`:
the message, a hint and the `.nuc` lines), up to three rounds; when Claude leads, it fixes what is left. The
step's *For the agent* tab shows what the agent read; *Output* keeps the real log.
The local agents only ever see Nuclear and the platform (backend, mobile, web), never Python, TypeScript or Dart.

**The chat (`Ctrl+Alt+A`, *Nuclear agent*).** A chat with the local agents, like Claude's or Cursor's: questions

model validates (`nuclear_check`, `dragonfly test`), corrects only what is wrong and records it with
`developer_review`, whose corrected files become examples in the graph for the local developer.

rows.title: AI loop: specs to deployed code, with local agents — 3. Follow the run
rows.summary: How the work is split, so the local 3B models only think the business logic:
body: | Actor | Does | Does not |
| You | write the spec, choose the context and the lead | write a piece here |
| Claude | plans, fixes what the local coder could not, teaches the graph | write every piece |
| Planner (gemma4:e2b) | splits a spec when no frontier model leads | make architecture decisions |
| Coder (qwen2.5-coder:3b) | writes one file at a time and repairs it with the compiler | choose names, data or architecture |
| Tester | writes the tests first, from the criteria and the plan; fixes a test file the project's check rejects | delete or weaken a failing test |
| Security | reviews each new file | change the code |
| Shell | runs the project's commands | run anything not in `.nuclear/loop.json` |

rows.title: AI loop: specs to deployed code, with local agents — 3. Follow the run
rows.summary: the reviewer, and every step with its agent, its trace and what the agent read.
body: **The journal.** Every run keeps `.nuclear/loop/runs/<id>.md` beside its `.json`: the files written, what is left for
the reviewer, and every step with its agent, its trace and what the agent read. At the end the local **documenter**
reads it and writes, at its top, what was built, how it was checked and what is left. A reviewer's notes go to
`<id>.review.md`.
**When it fails.** Calls to the local agents that fail for a passing reason are retried with exponential backoff
(the settings say how many and how long). When a stage fails, the local diagnoser tells why and what to do; *↻ Retry
from <stage>* (or `nuclear-loop retry <run>`, or the MCP tool `developer_retry`) runs it again from there.
**It survives the editor.** A run keeps a trace log, a heartbeat and a ledger of the files it writes: if VS Code closes
or crashes in the middle, the run is found interrupted when it opens again, what was left half written is undone, and
it goes on from that step. Every run first checks its connections (the Developer, the graph, Ollama and the models,
Claude when it leads, free disk); every few minutes every integration is checked again.
**It keeps working.** A run or a chat question does not stop when you switch tools or close its page; a notification
(and a badge on the Nuclear icon) tells you when it ends. *↻ Retry* goes on from the step that failed.

- **A node per step**, in the order it ran, and under it the steps its agent followed (recall from the graph, with

- **Click a node** and it opens beside the graph: what it did, **the decisions it took and why** (which strategy and
by which signs, why a piece was dropped or a file went to the tester), its input, its output and its code.

the analysis read in plain words ("each supplier has a name and a phone; we add and list them"), each call tried

"commands": {
"seed": ["dragonfly migrate", "python seed.py"],

rows.title: AI loop: specs to deployed code, with local agents — 5. How good is the local developer?
rows.summary: It is measured against Claude Sonnet on a bank of 45 tasks, 18 of them held out: 42 single files of every platform and 3 features of several files.
body: It is measured against Claude Sonnet on a bank of 45 tasks, 18 of them held out: 42 single files of every platform
and 3 features of several files. On single files the local 3B coder is at Sonnet's level (36 against 36). On whole
features it is behind: it passes one of the three by itself, while Sonnet passes all three. That is why Claude leads by default: it plans and fixes, the local developer writes the pieces. The
method, every round and every task are in
[the Developer's README](https://github.com/nuclearlang/nuclear-developer#evaluation-how-it-was-trained).

rows.title: AI loop: specs to deployed code, with local agents
rows.summary: NuclearLang ships three pieces for working with AI agents.
body: NuclearLang ships three pieces for working with AI agents. Together they take a spec to tested, reviewed code on your
machine, and the same pipeline can run on a server.
| Piece | What it is |

| [Nuclear Smart Graph](https://github.com/nuclearlang/nuclear-graph) | A private library of the whole ecosystem, as cards on shelves: what it is for, how each thing is written, every kind, tool and error, what can and cannot be done, how each task is done, validated code. Plus the **MCP server** (Model Context Protocol) of NuclearLang for Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. |

| [Nuclear Developer](https://github.com/nuclearlang/nuclear-developer) | Local agents on 3B models: a coder, a tester, a security reviewer and a planner. They search the graph and check their answers with the compiler. |

| **Loop** (VS Code `Ctrl+Alt+P`, Android Studio / IntelliJ `Alt+Shift+P`, `nuclear-loop` in a terminal or CI) | The pipeline: a spec goes through plan, code, tests, security, artifacts and deploy, and every step shows who did it. |
The idea: a frontier model like Claude makes the decisions (the plan, the names, the review), and the local developer
writes each piece. A lead hands work to a junior the same way. What the junior cannot fix, Claude fixes and keeps as
an example, so the junior gets it right next time.

```sh
claude mcp add --scope user nuclear -- nuclear-graph mcp   # Claude Code
codex mcp add nuclear -- nuclear-graph mcp                 # Codex
Cursor reads `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, OpenCode `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`:

What each group of tools needs running:

rows.summary: The server's instructions tell every client to call `graph_strategy` first, with the user's own words: it answers which kind of request it is and the plan of that kind (the strategies).
body: The server's instructions tell every client to call `graph_strategy` first, with the user's own words: it answers which
kind of request it is and the plan of that kind ([the strategies](loop.md#the-strategy-of-a-request)). For a feature
the plan is this order:

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — 2. How a model works with it
rows.summary: 1. Inspect.
body: 1. **Inspect.** `project_inspect`: what the project already has, so nothing is declared twice.
2. **Generate.** For every resource the spec names (a model and what is done with it), `generate_resource`. Its
fields come from the API's answer (`from_json`; `api_inspect` shows its shape first), from the spec (`from_spec`)
or from `fields`. When neither gives them, the model looks up the API's documentation (`web_search`, `web_read`)
and, if it is still unclear, asks the user: it never guesses. A use case that only calls a repository method is
`generate_usecase` with `calls`.
3. **The local developer writes the rest.** `developer_task` with what the generators did not write (a use case with
its own rules, a view's details): the local agents plan, write the tests first, write the code, run the tests and
the security review, and answer a journal of everything they did.
4. **Wire.** Each use case the local developer wrote, with `generate_usecase` (its alias in the facade, its route).
5. **Validate.** `nuclear_check` of the project must say `ok` and `dragonfly test` must pass.
6. **Correct only what failed**, never what passed. Before writing `.nuc` the model reads `nuclear_brief` and
searches the graph. A run that failed for a passing cause is run again with `developer_retry`.

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — 2. How a model works with it
rows.summary: 7. Review.
body: 7. **Review.** `developer_review` with what was corrected and why: the journal keeps it and the corrected files
become examples the local developer finds next time.
The model writes the code itself only when the local developer is not running, and says so.

generate_usecase(project, "orders", "CancelOrder", route="POST orders/{id}/cancel")   # CancelOrder is in the project
Nothing is overwritten and nothing is declared twice; `dry_run` shows the files first. A generator that cannot write
something finished refuses and says what to do: `generate_usecase` without `calls`, for a use case the project does
not declare, answers where to write it.

rows.summary: Generators
body: | Tool | What it does |
| `project_inspect(project)` | the project's platform and dialect, its components with their declarations by kind, the generators of its platform |
| `generate_component(project, component)` | a new component with its facade |

| `generate_resource(project, component, name, from_json \| from_spec \| fields, source, path, actions, screen, plural, dry_run)` | a resource: models, repository, a use case per action, the facade's aliases, the controller (backend) or a screen with its state manager (mobile, web), the tests |

| `generate_usecase(project, component, name, calls, route, dry_run)` | a use case wired into its component: its alias in the facade and, with `route` (backend), its route. With `calls` the use case is written too, because it only calls that repository method; without it the use case is one the project already has |
| `generate_screen(project, component, screen, route)` | mobile and web: a screen with its state manager and state model, for a view that is not a resource's list |

| `nuclear_build(code, dialect)` | what a piece of Nuclear becomes in the dialect's language |
| `nuclear_fmt(code)` | the piece in the canonical layout |
| `nuclear_help(word, dialect)` | the documentation of a kind, a decorator, a topic or a command |

| `dragonfly(project, command, args)` | `new`, `build`, `install`, `test`, `check`, `analyze`, `make`, `gen`, `migrate`, `add`, `explain` in a project |

body: | Tool | What it does |

body: | Tool | What it does |

| `developer_task(project, title, description, criteria, use_case)` | **the first step of every task that writes `.nuc`**: the local agents do the whole task in the project (plan, tests first, code, verification, security, artifacts) and answer the run's journal. `use_case`: `feature`, `bug`, `refactor`, `test` |

What the steps left out wrote is undone first |
| `developer_review(project, run, notes, files)` | **the last step**: the lead's corrections, kept in the journal; each corrected file goes to the graph's examples |
| `developer_code(task, platform, path, kind, context, project)` | one `.nuc` file outside a task, written, checked and repaired by the local model. It returns the file; it does not write it |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang
rows.summary: MCP is the Model Context Protocol: an AI client (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode) starts a program and calls the tools it offers.
body: MCP is the **Model Context Protocol**: an AI client (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode) starts a program and calls
the tools it offers. `nuclear-graph mcp` is that program for NuclearLang. It speaks MCP over stdio and gives a
frontier model four things: the **generators** that write the standard code, the **local developer** that writes what
is left, the **Smart Graph** to look things up instead of guessing, and the **compiler** to check everything.
The server also tells the model how to work, so every client behaves the same: generate first, let the local
developer write the rest, then validate and correct.

rows.title: Set up the AI services — 2. The steps
rows.summary: 1. This machine.
body: 1. **This machine.** The processor, the memory, the GPU and the free disk, and where the agents run: on this machine
(suggested: local agents write the code, so your remote agent spends tokens only on leading and correcting) or
remote agents only.
2. **The profile.** Which models are downloaded. One is suggested for your memory and disk; the ones that are tight
or do not fit are marked, with the reason. The choice is yours.
3. **What it needs.** Each program is found by itself once installed, or installed for you in a terminal you see:
| Program | For | Installed for you with |
| NuclearLang | the compiler, `dragonfly`, the code of the services | its installer |
| [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) | the Python environments of the services (it brings its own Python) | its installer, in your user folder |
| [Ollama](https://ollama.com) | running the local models | its own installer on Linux (it asks for your password), Homebrew on macOS, `winget` on Windows |
Without Ollama there are no local agents: install it, or go back and choose the remote agents only.
4. **Install.** The Smart Graph and the MCP server, the Nuclear Developer, the models, the knowledge base loaded
into the graph (about two minutes the first time), and both services started. A step that fails says why and is
tried again from there.

- **The plan knows the project.** With the project's folder (`root`), a declaration the project already has and the
spec only uses (`repository: BookRepository`) is not planned again; one the spec introduces with its kind's word ("a
repository BookRepository with...") is planned as a change of its file; and new pieces go to the component of the
declarations the spec uses, whatever component the model names.
The whole toolbox of an agent is one row of the graph, `service:agent-toolbox`: the graph, the compiler, the
`dragonfly` commands, the project's files and the internet.
What an agent reads is not a search over documents: the graph is a library of cards (ADR-0104). The coder asks for
`kind:<platform>.<kind>` by its id, for the pitfalls whose `kinds` list has that kind, for solved tasks and an example
file of that kind; a repair asks for `error:<code>` of each code the compiler named; the assistant searches every
shelf with the question and gets each card with the rows it links to; the diagnoser gets the cards of the codes in a
log and the closest known failures.

rows.title: Nuclear Developer — What it knows
rows.summary: The knowledge base of the whole project is `data/`: its own repository (`nuclear-knowledge`), rows on nine shelves: what NuclearLang is for, how each thing is written, every kind and decorator, every tool (the four CLIs, the MCP tools, the generators), every diagnostic and failure with its fix,…
body: The knowledge base of the whole project is [`data/`](data/README.md): its own repository (`nuclear-knowledge`), rows
on nine shelves: what NuclearLang is for, how each thing is written, every kind and decorator, every tool (the four
CLIs, the MCP tools, the generators), every diagnostic and failure with its fix, what can and cannot be done, how
each task is done step by step, and validated code. Most rows are generated from the working tree; the rest are
written by hand and reviewed when their sources change. The Smart Graph ingests it; the agents read every row but
the ones about the target languages and the dialects underneath (`agents: false`). After a change:
`nuclear-graph knowledge build`, `knowledge check`, then `nuclear-graph ingest`; `nuclear-graph knowledge ask` asks
the graph the questions people ask.

rows.title: Nuclear Developer — Where it works
rows.summary: ledger of the files it writes; an orphaned run is recovered (its unfinished step's files undone) and goes on from that step.
body: **When the editor closes in the middle.** A run keeps a trace log (`.nuclear/loop/runs/<id>.log`), a heartbeat and a
ledger of the files it writes; an orphaned run is recovered (its unfinished step's files undone) and goes on from that
step. A call to the Developer nothing works on (the Developer silent, Ollama holding no model) is cut and retried, and
every run first checks that the Developer, the graph, Ollama and the models it needs answer.
**What the agents may read.** Only Nuclear and the platform (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`): a row the agents read
has no target-language code (the build of the knowledge base refuses one that has), a failing test reaches them told in `.nuc` terms, a piece's errors are given by
line, and the diagnoser's prompt forbids speaking of the generated code.

rows.title: Nuclear Developer — Where it works
rows.summary: summary (what it built, how it checked it, what is left), why it failed (the diagnoser), the files written, what is left for the reviewer, and each step with its agent, its trace and what it read; a frontier model's review is `<id>.review.md`.
body: **Every run is documented.** `.nuclear/loop/runs/<id>.md` (beside the `.json` with every log whole): the documenter's
summary (what it built, how it checked it, what is left), why it failed (the diagnoser), the files written, what is
left for the reviewer, and each step with its agent, its trace and what it read; a frontier model's review is
`<id>.review.md`.
**When something fails.** A call to the Developer that fails for a passing reason (down, busy, 408/425/429/5xx) is
retried by its caller with exponential backoff and full jitter (5 tries, 1–30 s by default; `Retry-After` wins); a
compiler error or a failing test is never retried blindly — it goes to the repair rounds, then to the diagnoser (kind by
rules: transient, environment, code, test, spec; evidence from `nuclear check` or `dragonfly doctor`; the next step).
A failed run goes on from the step that failed (*↻ Retry*, `nuclear-loop retry <run>`, `developer_retry`): every step
that passed is kept, the earlier attempt stays in the run file.

rows.title: Nuclear Developer — Where it works
rows.summary: Where it works
body: | Who calls it | How | What the Developer does |

| The **Loop** (VS Code `Ctrl+Alt+P`, Android Studio *Nuclear Loop*, `nuclear-loop run`) | spec → plan → tests first → code → verification → security → artifacts → deploy | the planner splits the spec, the tester writes the tests first (and fixes a test file the project rejects), the coder writes each piece and repairs it with the compiler and with failing tests told in Nuclear (`dragonfly explain`), the security reviewer reads each new file; when a stage fails the **diagnoser** says why; at the end the **documenter** writes the journal's summary |

| The **chat** (VS Code `Ctrl+Alt+A`, *Nuclear agent*) | a question, or `/task <order>` | the **assistant** answers from the project's map and the graph; an order is a Loop run with the local agents only |

| A **frontier model** over MCP (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor: `nuclear-graph mcp`) | `developer_task` first, then validate, correct, `developer_review`; `developer_retry` after a failure | the whole task by the local agents (`nuclear-loop run --lead local`), documented in the run's journal; the lead's corrected files become graph examples |

rows.title: AGENTS.md — nuclear-graph
rows.summary: The Nuclear Smart Graph: the private library of NuclearLang and Dragonfly (one Chroma collection per shelf of typed, linked rows; EmbeddingGemma; the exact facts in SQLite, in memory), its HTTP server with access control, and the MCP server of the ecosystem.
body: The Nuclear Smart Graph: the private library of NuclearLang and Dragonfly (one Chroma collection per shelf of typed,
linked rows; EmbeddingGemma; the exact facts in SQLite, in memory), its HTTP server with access control, and the MCP
server of the ecosystem. Read README.md first; the decisions are ADR-0104 (the library), ADR-0107 (the exact facts and
the query planner; the graph written in Nuclear) and ADR-0102 (the AI loop) of the `nuclear` repository.
**It is written in Nuclear** (the `python` dialect; `nuclear.toml`): the `.nuc` files of this folder are the source,
`nuclear build .` writes the Python package into `build/nuclear_graph` (never edited, never committed) and
`pyproject.toml` packages that folder. After a change: `nuclear check .`, `nuclear build .`, the tests. What Nuclear
cannot express is a finding of the compiler for `../STATUS.md`, never a `.py` file written by hand.
This repository is a folder of the NuclearLang working tree (`nuclear/nuclear-graph`); the platform's rules are the
working tree's `../AGENTS.md` and its state is `../STATUS.md`.

body: What the graph knows is one folder: `nuclear-developer/data` (its own repository, `nuclear-knowledge`). Its

- **Generated rows** (`"origin": "generated"`, never edited by hand) are read from a structured source by

rows.summary: cards; the names the query writes (`N0114`, `gen resource`, `usecase`, `mcp`) are looked up in the cards' keys, so a code or a command reaches its card whatever the rest of the sentence says, in any language; a card is also found by the questions its author wrote for it.
body: **Search** is by meaning and by exact name at once: the query is embedded once and each shelf answers its closest
cards; the names the query writes (`N0114`, `gen resource`, `usecase`, `mcp`) are looked up in the cards' keys, so a
code or a command reaches its card whatever the rest of the sentence says, in any language; a card is also found by
the questions its author wrote for it. The search is exact: the stored vector of every item a filter matches is
compared with the query's (the store's own index is approximate and is not asked). A card is read directly by its id, with a line for each card it links to.
```sh
nuclear-graph search "como funciona el MCP"                # every shelf
nuclear-graph search "how do I declare an entity" -c platforms -p backend --agents
nuclear-graph card error:N0114                             # one card and what it links to
**A strategy** is the row of one kind of request a user makes (`strategy:resource-db`, `strategy:refactor-rename`,
`strategy:bug-failing-test`...: 31 of them, ADR-0105). `nuclear-graph strategy` says which one a request is, and why.
It asks no model: an exact sign of the request (a diagnostic code, a test's output, `rename A to B`, a `GET <url>`
line) outweighs any closeness of meaning, and meaning decides when there is none.

rows.title: Nuclear Smart Graph — Exact facts and the query planner
rows.summary: A search by meaning gives the closest cards, never *all* of something: asked for every tool of the MCP server, it gives four cards and a model fills in the rest.
body: A search by meaning gives the closest cards, never *all* of something: asked for every tool of the MCP server, it
gives four cards and a model fills in the rest. So the graph also holds **the exact facts** of the base in a relational
database (SQLite): every row's names, summary, links and structured fields (`meta`, `data`), with a view per thing a
question can list (`commands`, `mcp_tools`, `mcp_params`, `routes`, `kinds`, `decorators`, `plugins`, `generator_pieces`,
`diagnostics`, `library`, `stages`, `agents`, `components`, `strategies`...). The database lives in the memory of the
graph's process only: it is made from the cards the store keeps sealed when the graph starts, and again at every
ingest; nothing of it is written to disk, and it holds no row's body and nothing an agent kept at run time.

rows.summary: The `queries` shelf is the catalogue: one row per question with one right answer (`query:mcp.tools`, `query:mcp.group`, `query:kind.create`, `query:cli.commands`, `query:diagnostic`...), with the ways people ask it, its parameters (each with the query that lists the words people write and the…
body: The `queries` shelf is the catalogue: one row per question with one right answer (`query:mcp.tools`, `query:mcp.group`,
`query:kind.create`, `query:cli.commands`, `query:diagnostic`...), with the ways people ask it, its parameters (each
with the query that lists the words people write and the value each means: `generadores` → `generate`, `caso de uso` →
`usecase`) and its SQL, checked at build time against the views. **The planner** (`POST /v1/answer`, `nuclear-graph
answer "<question>"`, MCP `graph_answer`) asks no model: it matches the question to the catalogue (by meaning and by
the names it writes), fills the parameters from the question's own words (or, for a follow-up, from the user's earlier
messages), runs the queries, and searches the shelves for what is left. The shelves also decide whether a question is
exact at all: a query runs only when its exact question is closer to what was asked than the closest card, so "what is
nuclear" gets the card of the language and not the commands of the tool of that name. It answers `facts` (the rows,
whole), `knowledge` (the cards) and `needs` (an exact question it is close to that lacks a name). The local assistant
explains them, and the rows end its answer as they are, put there by code: a list never depends on a model.

body: The way to work, which the server's instructions give every client (Sonnet, Opus, Haiku, Codex...): **the local
developer works first, the frontier model validates and corrects.** For a feature it first inspects the project and
generates every resource the spec names (`generate_resource`, the fields from the spec, the API's answer or its
documentation, or the user when none gives them); then it calls `developer_task` for what is left and wires each
use case it wrote with `generate_usecase`; reads the
journal the local agents wrote (what each agent did, the files, what is left); validates with `nuclear_check` and
`dragonfly test`; corrects only what failed or is wrong; and records its review with `developer_review`, so the journal
keeps it and the local developer learns the corrected files. It writes the code itself only when the local developer
is not running. `developer_code` stays for one quick file outside a task.

rows.title: Nuclear Smart Graph — Who may read it
rows.summary: constant time, and an allowed request hands its token once; (`secret-tool`, libsecret), or in `0600` files of the data folder when there is no keyring; a graph that starts while its keyring is closed (a service at login) waits for it and never makes a second key or token; documentation.
body: - the server listens on `127.0.0.1` only; a request with an `Origin` header (a web page) is refused;
- every route but `/v1/health` and the access request needs a token; tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes, compared in
constant time, and an allowed request hands its token once;
- documents are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM); the key and the owner token live in the desktop keyring
(`secret-tool`, libsecret), or in `0600` files of the data folder when there is no keyring; a graph that starts
while its keyring is closed (a service at login) waits for it and never makes a second key or token;
- the data folder (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/nuclear-graph`, `0700`) is opened only by the server process;
- only `ingest` writes the shelves of the base: a client writes `memory` and `examples` and cannot plant false
documentation.
Limits: protection is per OS user. A program running as you could ask the keyring for the key as the graph does; the
graph stops other users, web pages and programs that only speak HTTP or MCP. The vectors and the metadata (ids,
titles, keys) are stored in clear (Chroma searches them): they reveal what a row is about, not its text.

rows.summary: 1. A task generator, not hand-written tasks.
body: 1. **A task generator, not hand-written tasks.** The platforms already describe every kind (`docs.toml`, `[layout]`,
`[skeletons]`, the briefs): a script crosses kinds × business domains (library, shop, clinic, school…) × variations
(fields, relations, rules, errors) into thousands of task texts with acceptance texts.
2. **Answers validated by NuclearLang itself.** Every answer must pass `nuclear check` (as a project for features) and
its acceptance texts; nothing else enters the dataset. Wrong answers with their errors become repair pairs.
3. **Where the answers come from — to decide with the user:**
- *Self-distillation* (no external terms): the local model samples many answers per task, the compiler keeps the
ones that pass, and those train the next round (rejection sampling). Free, slower to start.
- *A frontier model*: Claude answers the tasks (≈ USD 0.02–0.03 per answer with Sonnet: ≈ USD 100–300 for 5–10k;
the user approved USD 20 so far). **Before using Claude's answers as training data, check Anthropic's terms for
training models on outputs** (the commercial terms restrict building competing models).
- *The tree's own code*: every example, test and generated docs (`.nuclear/map.md` descriptions → their code).
